candidateRows: Reasonableness is distinct from personal conviction and must be judged by an objective standard for unusual beliefs.
This establishes the governing burden and meaning of reasonableness on which Trent's entire affirmative case depends.
At the start of his opening, Trent distinguishes a reasonable belief from one that personally convinces an individual and demands an objective standard.
Belief in an unusual event is reasonable when it contradicts no established subject-specific fact, lacks no expected evidence, and resists equally adequate ordinary explanations.
The three-part test supplies the affirmative's principal epistemic standard and directly determines its conclusion about resurrection belief.
Trent develops three tests for unusual claims, applies the first two to resurrection evidence, and explains the third through comparison with an Islamic miracle claim.
Historical testimony is evidence rather than merely an unsupported claim, and early sources indicate authentic experiences behind the disciples' resurrection proclamations.
This directly answers the objection that resurrection reports provide no evidence and supplies the historical basis for the affirmative case.
Matt's prior contention that resurrection materials are only claims and do not constitute evidence.
Trent compares resurrection testimony with ordinary historical evidence, then argues that Paul, Luke, early communities, and cited scholars support authentic experiences by early believers.
Legend, deceit, and hallucination do not explain the resurrection reports as readily as a real resurrection, while their distinctive character makes a supernatural explanation non-ad-hoc.
Eliminating ordinary alternatives and defending the relevance of divine agency performs the main inferential work from testimony to reasonable resurrection belief.
Ordinary explanations such as invention, dishonesty, hallucination, or an ad-hoc supernatural attribution.

Trent challenges deceit and hallucination accounts using Paul, James, group appearances, Jewish expectations, the empty tomb, and sincerity, then argues resurrection evidence specifically points toward divine agency.
A changing universe requires an unactualized cause of change whose attributes correspond to an immaterial, timeless, powerful, knowledgeable, necessary, good, and personal God.
The argument supplies background plausibility for the divine agency required by the resurrection explanation, though it is not itself historical evidence for resurrection.
Trent presents an argument from change, rejects an infinite derivative series as explanatory, and derives divine attributes from a cause characterized as pure actuality.
A claim is reasonable when it accords with what is known to be true and possible in reality, independently of whether the claim ultimately happens to be true.
This supplies the negative side's governing epistemic standard and frames all later objections concerning testimony, testability, and background knowledge.
Trent's proposed three-part standard for determining whether belief in an unusual event is reasonable.

Matt distinguishes truth from justified belief, notes that individuals and communities attempt to control bias, and grounds reasonableness in consistency with known reality rather than internal coherence.
The resurrection is supported only by hearsay rather than physical evidence, and an unverifiable, unfalsifiable, high-stakes extraordinary claim cannot reasonably ground a life-defining religion.
The move states the negative case's principal evidential objection and explains why the alleged evidence is insufficient for the importance and unusualness of the claim.
Trent's contention that the expected historical evidence exists and makes resurrection belief reasonable.

Matt contrasts testimony with physical evidence, stresses the claim's stakes, distinguishes verification from falsification, treats history as report-based and uncertain, and urges confidence proportioned to evidence.
When testimony reports a resurrection, deception, error, or distorted transmission is more probable than an event unsupported by evidence that such occurrences are possible.
This supplies the negative's comparative explanation for the reports and directly opposes the affirmative inference from testimony to an actual resurrection.
Trent's argument that ordinary mistakes, deception, and story development do not adequately explain the resurrection reports.
Matt explains that rejecting the less probable explanation does not require accepting another explanation outright, then favors mistake, deception, or inaccurate stories over resurrection.
Even eyewitness accounts would be inadequate because the sources cannot be identified, questioned, reconciled, or physically corroborated, whereas a capable God could have supplied decisive evidence.
The move attacks the reliability and sufficiency of the affirmative's historical sources while arguing that the expected evidence under divine agency is conspicuously absent.
Trent's reliance on early testimony, Gospel narratives, appearances, and expected historical traces as sufficient evidence.

Matt argues that unknown and inaccessible testimonial chains cannot establish resurrection, notes inconsistencies and absent physical corroboration, and says divine involvement raises the expected-evidence standard.
Common apologetic details do not strengthen the resurrection case, whose lack of physical evidence would fail ordinary contemporary standards and makes belief unreasonable.
This is an explicit motion-level application of the negative evidential standard and directly rejects claimed credibility-enhancing features of the resurrection narratives.
Theistic claims that miraculous framing and details such as women discovering the tomb increase the narratives' credibility.

Matt rejects attempts to infer truth from supposedly unlikely narrative details, compares the resulting case with untrustworthy pitches, and emphasizes the absence of physical findings or examinable witnesses.
Resurrection belief feels reasonable only after prior acceptance of supernatural claims that themselves cannot be confirmed.
The move directly challenges the background assumptions that make resurrection testimony seem credible and ties those assumptions to the motion's reasonableness standard.
Near the end of his opening, Dillahunty argues that emotional pressures and prior supernatural commitments, rather than adequate evidence, explain acceptance of the resurrection narrative.
Resurrection belief is unreasonable because there is insufficient physical evidence beyond testimonial accounts.
This is Dillahunty's direct answer to the motion and identifies the evidential deficiency on which his negative case principally rests.
Horn's request for a concise statement of why resurrection belief is unreasonable.
During Horn's cross-examination, Dillahunty condenses his position into the absence of sufficient and physical evidence, leaving only testimonial reports.
Claims that resurrections never occur are under-supported when numerous reported cases exist but have not been investigated.
The move attacks the empirical basis for treating resurrection as inconsistent with reality, a central premise in the opposing evidential standard.
Dillahunty's claim that resurrections do not happen and have never been confirmed.
Horn cites a large collection of reported resurrections and presses whether Dillahunty has investigated enough cases to justify a general denial.
If resurrections were established phenomena, scientific journals, major awards, and public demonstrations would document confirmed cases.
It supplies an absence-of-expected-evidence argument supporting the negative side's claim that current resurrection reports lack confirmation.
Horn's challenge that uninvestigated reports undermine the claim that resurrections do not occur.
Dillahunty argues that a genuinely demonstrated resurrection would leave conspicuous scientific and public records, then asks how many of Keener's cases were confirmed.
The negative case need only show that resurrection belief is not reasonable, not establish that the resurrection did not happen.
The move fixes the burden of proof for the debate and distinguishes withholding justified belief from affirmatively denying the historical event.
Horn's earlier characterization of Dillahunty's burden as challenging reasonable belief rather than proving nonoccurrence.
At the start of his questioning period, Dillahunty clarifies that he is unconvinced the event occurred and need not prove that it did not occur.
Using belief in Jesus's resurrection to establish that present resurrections are possible is circular and compounds an unsupported belief.
The response identifies circular dependence in the positive case's modal reasoning and denies that an assumed resurrection can validate comparable claims.
Horn's assertion that current resurrection reports are possible because Jesus rose from the dead.
When Horn grounds the possibility of modern resurrections in Jesus's resurrection, Dillahunty objects that the debated conclusion cannot serve as its own support.
Accepting suspension of the physical order for one person on testimony alone is an unreasonable and dangerously credulous epistemic standard.
The statement directly contrasts the competing standards for unusual testimony and delivers the negative side's central judgment on resurrection belief.
Horn's eventual concession that he can accept a resurrection on testimonial evidence alone.
After securing Horn's affirmative answer, Dillahunty states that their foundational disagreement is whether testimony can justify a miraculous exception to physical understanding.
Uniform natural laws make miracles identifiable rather than improbable, and reliable testimony can establish exceptions to prior uniform experience.
The move answers a major background-probability objection and argues that unusual testimonial evidence can rationally revise experience-based generalizations.
The moderator's challenge that uniformity of natural laws may count as evidence against miracles.
Horn uses a life-jacket contrast and the historical discovery of black swans to argue that regularity permits recognition of genuine exceptions supported by reliable testimony.
Testimony is reasonable only within established background knowledge, so mundane puppy testimony differs fundamentally from resurrection testimony.
This supplies the negative side's governing evidential principle and explains why ordinary testimonial reliability does not transfer to an extraordinary resurrection claim.
The moderator's question whether testimonial evidence alone can make a belief reasonable.
Dillahunty explains that apparently testimony-only acceptance of an ordinary claim actually relies on extensive prior evidence about how reality works.
Multiple sincere witnesses who accept costly punishment can make extraordinary testimony credible, as testimony also underwrites ancient history generally.
The move presents the positive side's principal justification for treating resurrection testimony as sufficient despite the event's unusual character.
Dillahunty's claim that testimony gains force only from background evidence consistent with ordinary reality.
Horn argues that the resurrection has unusually strong testimony from sincere early witnesses, strengthened by group attestation and willingness to suffer for the claim.
Not knowing in advance what evidence would be sufficient is compatible with recognizing that the evidence presented so far has not been sufficient.
This establishes Dillahunty's central epistemic position on unspecified future evidence and explains why absence of a predetermined criterion does not require accepting current resurrection evidence.
Horn's challenge that Dillahunty cannot reject the evidence without specifying what sufficient resurrection evidence would look like.

Horn asks whether Dillahunty has no idea what sufficient resurrection evidence would be while remaining confident that he has not encountered it; Dillahunty answers by comparing the issue to evidence for God.
If someone cannot identify what sufficient evidence would look like, that person may have already encountered it without recognizing it.
The move directly attacks the coherence of Dillahunty's evidential standard by arguing that an undefined recognition criterion undermines confidence that sufficient evidence has not appeared.
Dillahunty's claim that he does not know what would convince him while maintaining that the necessary evidence has not yet been provided.
Immediately after Dillahunty says he cannot predetermine what would convince him, Horn argues that ignorance of the identifying features leaves open the possibility that the evidence was missed.
An epistemology focused on avoiding false beliefs can do so at the cost of rejecting reasonable true historical beliefs supported only by testimony.
This challenges Dillahunty's governing standard as excessively skeptical and connects that alleged false-negative bias directly to how unusual historical claims based on testimony should be assessed.
Dillahunty's courtroom-based epistemology of believing as many true things and as few false things as possible.

The speakers debate whether minimizing false belief conflicts with maximizing true belief; Horn resumes after a technical interruption and tests the issue with Josephus's singular, biased testimony about Masada.
Neither truth nor reasonableness is determined by how many historians or other people accept a proposition.
The move rejects consensus as a sufficient measure of reasonable belief, undercutting Horn's attempt to establish historical bedrock through near-unanimous scholarly acceptance.
Horn's appeal to historians at major universities and the marginal status of views denying Jesus's crucifixion.

Horn invokes broad academic agreement that Jesus existed and died by crucifixion while excluding fringe or institutionally marginal positions; Dillahunty responds that head counts do not establish truth or reasonableness.
Investigation cannot extend beyond material reality until the supernatural is demonstrated and made available as a field of inquiry.

This supplies the con side's core methodological objection: supernatural resurrection explanations cannot become warranted candidates merely by being asserted before their domain or investigability is demonstrated.
Horn's suggestion that science can test only material entities within the space-time universe and may therefore exclude supernatural realities.

After defining science as investigation toward the best available explanation, the exchange turns to its scope; Dillahunty argues that any demonstrated supernatural domain would itself become subject to systematic inquiry.
The resurrection case rests on ordinary historical judgments that Jesus lived, died, and was later seen alive, so biblical documents should not be disqualified merely for being biblical.
The passage condenses Horn's affirmative case and defends the admissibility of its principal testimony, linking general historical reasoning directly to the resurrection conclusion.
Dillahunty's account of credible historical testimony and his preference for agreement involving independent or opposing sources.

Following discussion of how agreement between proponents and opponents can support historical claims, Horn restates the resurrection sequence and challenges treating biblical writings as categorically inferior evidence.
Elvis sightings have established counterevidence and ordinary alternatives that are absent from the reports that Jesus was seen alive after death.

The comparison answers an important parody objection by identifying evidential differences rather than relying only on the rarity of resurrection, thereby defending differential treatment of the two reports.
Dillahunty's challenge that reports of Elvis after his death should be treated like claims that Jesus was seen alive after death.

Dillahunty invokes postmortem Elvis sightings; after discussion of faked death and the availability of Elvis's body, Horn emphasizes contrary physical evidence, medical testimony, and familiar misidentification mechanisms.
Horn's resurrection belief is falsifiable in principle, with strong contrary identification evidence or an early apostolic recantation capable of seriously undermining it.

The answer clarifies the affirmative side's falsifiability conditions and distinguishes weakly identified remains from historically decisive counterevidence concerning Jesus or apostolic proclamation.
The audience question asking whether verified bones of Jesus would end Horn's Catholic or Christian belief and alter his belief in God.

During audience questions, Horn says falsifying Christianity would move him toward another supported worldview, discusses identification problems with alleged remains, and names apostolic recantation evidence as severely damaging.
A willingness to die demonstrates strength or presentation of belief, not the truth of the religious proposition for which someone dies.
The move blocks a major inference from apostolic sacrifice to resurrection truth by separating sincerity from accuracy and applying the distinction across competing religious commitments.
The audience argument that apostles and later Christians would not willingly accept death unless the gospel and resurrection were true.

Asked why apostles and later Christians would die if the gospel were false, Dillahunty notes that deception need not be conscious and that adherents of many incompatible religions have accepted death.
Apostolic persecution supports sincerity rather than truth directly, but their sincere resurrection belief still requires an explanation for which resurrection is the best account.
This preserves the martyrdom evidence in a narrower but crucial role: it supports sincere apostolic conviction, which Horn then joins to his broader explanatory case for resurrection.
Dillahunty's argument that willingness to die indicates conviction but has no bearing on whether the underlying resurrection claim is actually true.

Horn briefly addresses the Waco example, agrees that dying for a claim does not prove it, then argues that evidence of costly apostolic perseverance establishes sincerity and raises the question of its cause.
The disciples’ willingness to endure persecution supports their sincerity, and resurrection best explains that sincere belief.
The move connects testimony about costly commitment to the sincerity of the disciples and then to the resurrection as its best explanation.
Matt’s position that willingness to die demonstrates conviction but has no bearing on whether the underlying belief is true.
Following discussion of Waco and religious martyrdom, Trent concedes that sacrifice does not prove truth but argues that it establishes sincere belief requiring explanation.
Claims that God should have arranged modern evidence are unsupported, while the available historical evidence can still make resurrection belief reasonable.
The response addresses expected evidence and divine timing, both central to whether the historically available resurrection case is reasonable.
The objection that Jesus appearing in modern times would permit better documentation and therefore reveal poor timing in the historical account.
Asked why Jesus did not appear in an era of video recording, Trent challenges assumptions about what evidence God would provide and redirects attention to assessing the evidence available.
A God who wants universal relationship could provide better evidence, and sufficient evidence capable of convincing Matt has not been supplied.
The move directly contests the adequacy of expected evidence and rebuts the claim that disbelief merely reflects an excessively high evidential bar.
Trent’s claim that demands for different evidence are unsupported and that some skeptics may have set their evidential threshold too high.
Matt distinguishes what God could provide from predictions about what God would provide, then argues that a relational God has both the capacity and reason to provide convincing evidence.
Without prior warrant that God guarantees scripture, biblical resurrection accounts must be treated as fallible sources rather than divinely certified testimony.
This challenges the reliability foundation of the affirmative historical case and explains how background beliefs about God can determine the treatment of biblical testimony.
Trent’s account that prior belief in a capable theistic God made the historical resurrection evidence more plausible to him.
Matt recalls formerly accepting the Bible as reliable because God supposedly preserved it, but says losing that premise required treating its writings like other potentially biased sources.
Reasonableness is a lower standard than personal conviction, permitting reasonable disagreement among competing historical explanations.
The distinction defines the affirmative burden in the motion and resists evaluating resurrection belief solely by whether it personally convinces the opponent.
Matt’s defense of his own evidential standards and the suggestion that each person must judge reasonableness through those standards.
Trent uses competing explanations of the Mary Celeste to argue that more than one conclusion can remain reasonable, then invokes his three-part framework for evaluating possibilities.
People considering the same information cannot reasonably disagree if one argument genuinely compels the rational conclusion; an unconvinced person is unreasonable on that subject.
The move supplies the negative side’s competing account of the debate’s key standard and directly challenges the affirmative distinction between reasonable and convincing.
Trent’s claim that reasonableness falls below conviction and allows rational people to disagree over competing historical explanations.

Matt accepts that added documentation would improve the resurrection case, then argues that identical information should not rationally yield opposed conclusions once an argument is genuinely reasonable.
Evidence requires interpretation, and resurrection belief can be reasonable when it does not contradict established facts or expected evidence and lacks a usual alternative explanation.
The move articulates the affirmative’s operative test for reasonable belief and argues that Matt has not supplied a determinate threshold for resurrection evidence.
Matt’s claim that anyone left unconvinced by a reasonable argument is necessarily out of accord with reason on that particular subject.
Trent argues that raw facts do not announce their conclusions, illustrates interpretive limits with courtroom evidence, and restates his criteria for judging a belief reasonable.
Historical belief need not meet courtroom or absolute-certainty standards, and the evidential burden does not increase merely because resurrection belief affects one’s life.
The response addresses standards of proof, historical justification, degrees of certainty, and whether existential consequences should alter the evidence required by the motion.
Matt’s explanation that fallible measuring tools prevent absolute certainty while still allowing extremely confident rejection of erroneous conclusions.

Trent draws an analogy between limited measurement and historical inquiry, argues that historical methods can justify belief without courtroom proof, and rejects outcome-sensitive evidential thresholds.
Even unanimous sincere testimony would establish widespread belief rather than resurrection, because ordinary error remains less extraordinary than a violation of established experience.
The move directly addresses whether testimony alone can reasonably establish resurrection and states the negative side’s comparative standard for extraordinary claims.
The hypothetical challenge asking whether testimony from everyone else in the world would make belief in a witnessed death and resurrection reasonable.

Matt distinguishes trusting witnesses’ sincerity from accepting their interpretation, illustrates the distinction through his mother’s reported experience, and favors mistake over a supernatural event.
Testimony should be assessed by its supporting reasons, while treating uniform experience as a bar to unusual events risks false beliefs and imports contested assumptions about nature.
The response directly challenges the negative side’s Humean standard, defends inquiry into unusual testimony, and disputes naturalistic assumptions governing the resurrection assessment.
Matt’s argument that sincere testimony does not establish extraordinary events because mistake is more consistent with demonstrated uniform experience.
Trent agrees that popularity alone is weak support, then argues that evidence behind testimony matters and that unfamiliar phenomena or widespread reports cannot be dismissed by local experience.
Widespread reports of ghosts and immaterial beings count against treating laboratory testability or presumed natural uniformity as grounds for dismissing supernatural experience.
The move challenges the con side's evidential treatment of supernatural testimony and the background assumption that nature excludes such events.
Matt's refusal to credit reported demonic experiences and his appeal to uniform natural experience.
Continuing a discussion of Humean uniformity, Trent turns to reported immaterial experiences and argues that their prevalence cannot be dismissed merely because they resist laboratory testing.
Testimony is a legitimate source of knowledge when supplemented as needed by investigation of the underlying evidence.
The proposition supplies the pro side's basic epistemic defense of relying on historical testimony while still permitting further evidential scrutiny.
Trent frames the fundamental dispute as one about methods for finding truth and uses ordinary acquisition of historical knowledge to defend testimony as an evidential source.
Science is one truth-seeking tool among several, is suited to explaining natural regularities, and remains provisional rather than exhaustive.
The move disputes an exclusively scientific evidential standard that would exclude historical or supernatural conclusions before their particular evidence is considered.
Matt's stated science bias and reliance on scientific methods for understanding reality.
Using detectors suited to different objects, the replication crisis, and the abandonment of phrenology, Trent argues for methodological pluralism and provisional scientific knowledge.
The resurrection remains a reasonable live possibility because God could raise Jesus and Trent's proposed three-part test was not falsified.
This directly asserts that the resurrection satisfies the pro side's standard of reasonable belief and that a divine explanation remains available.
Matt's case that the resurrection claim is unreasonable under the available evidence and background knowledge.
After conceding caution toward unique claims, Trent says his three-part test survived the debate and invokes his argument for God to preserve divine resurrection as an explanatory option.
Matt's undefined sufficient-evidence standard risks circularity and, if sufficiency merely means causing belief, can equally vindicate resurrection belief.
The move attacks the determinacy and consistency of the con side's evidential threshold, a central point governing whether resurrection belief is reasonable.
Matt's claim that sufficient evidence would convince him despite not specifying what such evidence would look like.
Trent argues that an unspecified standard could overlook available evidence and that defining sufficiency by whether evidence causes belief would also validate believers' evidence.
The con burden is to show that accepting the resurrection is unreasonable, not to establish that the resurrection is false.
The distinction defines the con side's burden on the exact motion and separates warranted acceptance from the independent truth value of the resurrection claim.
Trent's characterization of Matt's burden and evidential obligations in arguing against reasonable resurrection belief.
Matt clarifies that he need only undermine the reasonableness of accepting the proposition and need not prove that the proposition itself is false.
Rejecting extraordinary historical claims does not discard history generally, and supernatural-experience reports better demonstrate human fallibility than a supernatural reality.
It answers both the charge that skepticism destroys historical knowledge and the pro inference from accumulated supernatural testimony to a supernatural world.
The objections that skepticism about resurrection discards history and that many supernatural reports attest to supernatural reality.

Matt distinguishes routine historical conclusions from claims conflicting with established reality, then interprets supernatural anecdotes as evidence of mistaken human inference rather than supernatural ontology.
Not knowing what evidence would convince him of God does not mean Matt missed it, because an existing God could present unmistakable evidence.
The move rebuts the pro side's claim that an unspecified threshold makes nonbelief evidentially defective and locates the explanatory burden with a capable deity.
Trent's argument that Matt could have missed sufficient evidence because he cannot specify what would convince him.
Matt says a deity necessarily capable of convincing him could make the evidence unmissable, so continued nonbelief is compatible with honesty despite an unspecified evidential form.
Ancient resurrection testimony is weaker than evidence available for an equivalent present-day claim because temporal distance sharply limits investigation.
The move directly evaluates the quality of the historical evidence central to the motion and explains why numerous attestations do not overcome investigative limitations.
Trent's reliance on testimony and historical evidence to support the reasonableness of an ancient resurrection claim.
Matt compares resurrection testimony with contemporary claims about miraculous survival and healing, arguing that moving a claim into the distant past reduces the means of checking it.
Scientific methods remain the most consistently reliable way to understand reality, while the historical case supplies no adequate substitute or physical support for Jesus's resurrection.
The move states the con side's ultimate methodological and evidential basis for denying that the specific resurrection conclusion is reasonably supported.
Trent's methodological pluralism, criticism of scientific failures, and appeal to historical argument for the resurrection.
Matt argues that science corrects its own errors, denies that supernatural claims have corrected science, rejects assumed scriptural reliability, and concludes that physical support is absent.
